summary: Captures the rationale for the changes made in RFC 8714. It gives background on past IETF Trust arrangements, in which IAOC members served as trustees, and why the move to IASA 2.0 required a new approach to selecting trustees.

plainLanguage.summary: This is the reasons note for a rule change about who looks after the IETF's property, explaining why the old setup had to go.

questions: why change ietf trust trustee selection
subtitle: Why the IETF changed how it selects trustees for the IETF Trust.

tldr.problem: The IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) was being phased out as part of IASA 2.0 restructuring, but members of the IAOC also served as Trustees of the IETF Trust, which holds intellectual property and domain names.
tldr.mechanism: Rather than merge the IETF Trust into the new IASA 2.0 structure, the IETF decided to keep it independent and change how Trustees are selected, appointing them through the NomCom, IESG, and Internet Society instead of through IAOC membership.
tldr.outcome: The Trust continues to function independently with a smaller, more specialized group of Trustees whose qualifications and term lengths can be tailored to the Trust's needs rather than driven by other administrative requirements.

today: RFC 8715 is an Informational document that explains the rationale behind RFC 8714, which updated the IETF Trust Trustee selection process when IASA 2.0 was introduced in 2020. Both RFCs remain the current basis for how the IETF Trust Trustees are selected.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: RFC 8715 explains why the IETF changed the way it selects Trustees for the IETF Trust. This companion document provides the reasoning behind the changes introduced in RFC 8714. The IETF Trust is the legal entity that holds and manages intellectual property rights, domain names (including ietf.org), and trademarks associated with the IETF. When the IETF reorganized its administrative structure through IASA 2.0, the Trust's governance needed adjustment because the previous Trustees had been members of the IAOC, which was being discontinued.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF Trust owns important things like copyrights and domain names. When the IETF changed its management structure, someone had to explain why they were changing who picks the people to look after the Trust.

sections.title: The IETF Trust and the IAOC
sections.content:
The IETF Trust is a legal entity registered in Virginia that acquires, holds, maintains, and licenses property used in connection with IETF administration. This includes intellectual property rights that IETF contributors grant for RFCs and Internet-Drafts, as well as trademarks like "IETF" and domain names like "ietf.org". The Trust also manages domains and trademarks associated with IANA.

Historically, the members of the IETF Administrative Oversight Committee (IAOC) also served as ex officio Trustees of the IETF Trust. The IAOC had eight voting members plus three ex officio members (the IETF Chair, ISOC CEO, and IAB Chair). However, when the IETF restructured to IASA 2.0, the IAOC was being phased out, leaving the Trust without a clear appointment mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF Trust is a special company that owns things the IETF needs, like its website and copyrights. The people who ran the IETF's other business were also in charge of the Trust. But when the IETF changed how it was run, those people were going away, so someone needed a new way to pick Trust leaders.

sections.title: Why Keep the Trust Independent
sections.content:
Rather than merge the IETF Trust into the new IASA 2.0 structure, the RFC advocates for keeping the Trust independent. This decision was based on the recognition that the IETF Trust and the broader IETF administrative processes are fundamentally different. The Trust is a low-activity entity with minimal, gradual changes and no pressing issues, whereas the IETF administrative structure undergoes frequent reorganization and change.

By keeping the Trust separate, the IETF could minimize disruption to the Trust during a major restructuring of the administrative organization. This approach also allows the Trust to have leadership selected for the specific needs of managing intellectual property and assets, rather than having its Trustee composition driven by the requirements of other IETF administrative functions.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF could have made the Trust part of the new management structure, but it decided not to. The Trust runs smoothly and does not change much, so keeping it separate meant it would not get tangled up in the big reorganization.

sections.title: The New Selection Process
sections.content:
Under the new arrangement, Trustees are appointed through three separate channels: the IETF Nominating Committee (NomCom), the IESG, and the Internet Society Board of Trustees. This approach reuses the successful principle of having the NomCom appoint some Trustees with confirmation by the IESG (which had previously confirmed IAOC appointments).

The RFC notes that earlier approaches had considered continuing to use the IETF Chair, IAB Chair, and ISOC CEO as ex officio Trustees, but rejected this on the grounds that the Trust's tasks are well-defined and do not require engagement at the level of organizational chairs or CEOs. Instead, a smaller, more specialized group of Trustees is appropriate. The flexibility to set longer term lengths for Trustees (compared to the typical two-year terms of other IETF bodies) reflects the Trust's stable, long-term stewardship needs.
sections.plainLanguage: The new way picks Trustees from three different places: the IETF's regular nomination process, its leadership, and the Internet Society. The RFC explains why this makes sense and why it does not need the top leaders to be in charge of the Trust.

sections.title: Managing the Change
sections.content: The RFC notes that during the transition when IASA 2.0 was being set up and the IAOC was still being phased out, there was no pressing need to change all components at once. The IESG was given the authority to continue naming Trustees in an exception process during this transition period, ensuring continuity of the Trust's governance. Once the updated procedures were fully in place and regular NomCom appointments began, this temporary exception process would no longer be needed.
sections.plainLanguage: The change did not have to happen all at once. While things were still being reorganized, the IESG could pick temporary trustees to keep things running. Once the new system was ready, the normal appointment process took over.
